items_missed: Never got or used the customer's name. The call opened 'Hello, this is ran with Einstein. How can I help you?' and Rance identified the record by email ('what was the email address you used to submit your estimate') — Juan's name is never spoken once in 10.9 minutes, which also zeroes the 3+ name-use bullet in Politeness.
No 'how are you today?' — the customer actually asked Rance first ('Yeah. Hi how are you?') and it was never returned.

No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' — no roadmap, no 10-15 minute timeframe, no confirmation. Rance went straight from the email lookup into silent math ('One moment. Yeah, I'm gonna say the. Let's see. Sorry, one moment. I'm doing some math here').

Move-date availability never checked. He confirmed the date on file ('You're looking to move 913') but never said Einstein has that Sunday open — on a call where the customer volunteered 'I'm moving on next Sunday' and was actively shopping competitors, availability was the cheapest possible close and it was never offered.

DAY-OF-WEEK RATE FLAG: Rance quoted 'The hourly rate, it's Tuesday, 210 an hour.' The call was placed Sunday 9/6 and the move date on file (9/13) is also a Sunday. The Tuesday tier matches neither the call day nor the move day, so the entire quote — $210/hr for two, $315/hr for three, the $2,047 figure — may be built on the wrong rate tier. Needs verification in EMMA before the estimate email is trusted.

Never gave a dollar total for the two-mover option he actually recommended. He quoted 8-9 hours at $210/hr and then only produced a total for the three-mover scenario ('a $2,047 would be kind of a reasonable budget'). The customer was left doing arithmetic out loud — 'so 200. For 210 for two movers, 315 or so, for three movers estimated. Yeah, I can't see on eight hours.' The primary recommendation went un-priced.

Disassembly/reassembly never stated as included for Einstein. He named it only as a competitor's hidden fee ('assembly, disassemble fees') without ever closing the loop that Einstein includes it — and this customer has an expanding day bed, a dining table with chairs, and a 'working station' that all need breakdown.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — a notable miss given the customer flagged a reserved service elevator, which is a hard time window on both ends.
No 'no hidden fees' credit-card-fee or fuel-surcharge language. The pitch covered stairwell, assembly/disassembly, TV boxes and travel fees but stopped short of the full list.

Clock section almost entirely absent: no 'clock starts on-site when the contract opens' and no 2.5-hour minimum. He got the 15-minute increments right ('we're going to round it off to the nearest fifteen minute increment') but never explained when the clock starts — on a 32nd-floor origin where crew travel time inside the building is the whole cost story, start-of-clock is exactly what the customer needed defined.
No sense-check anywhere. Never 'does that make sense?' after the elevator math, after the rate, or after the objection response.
Walk distance / loading dock never probed. Both addresses are downtown Austin towers (215 Brazos, 101 Colorado) and the carry distance from dock to unit is a major time variable that went unasked.

COI and parking/loading-dock access never raised. Two high-rise buildings almost certainly require certificates of insurance and reserved dock windows; the customer only half-asked about it himself ('the elevator is gonna be reserved') and Rance answered 'Yup' without confirming who reserves it or whether a COI is needed.
No truck-capacity equivalent or school-bus reference, and no confirmation that a 2BR fits in one truck.
Traffic never mentioned despite a downtown-to-downtown move.

Save Your Ass speech never delivered. The customer handed him the setup verbatim — 'this is very close to where we are today. We we're going to be moving a lot of the stuff ourselves' — and Rance only validated it passively ('Luckily, if you're gonna move over a lot of the boxes that will kind of help a lot'). No consolidation examples (kids' toys, garden tools, loose items in drawers, photos off walls), no 'take a carload' tip, no 'does that make sense?' close. On an 8-9 hour elevator move, prep coaching was worth hundreds of dollars to this customer and would have been the strongest differentiator available.

No booking attempt at all. The customer said 'I'll finish the calls and, and if, you know, I decide to go with you guys and I'll give you guys a call later today to book it' and Rance replied 'Okay, sounds good.' No ask, no offer to hold the Sunday date, no specific follow-up time.

'No deposit required' never mentioned — the single most costly omission on a call where the customer's only stated objection was price ('you guys are like thirty percent more expensive'). A free hold answers a price objection and costs nothing.
Packing services never asked about or priced. The customer said he'd handle boxes himself, but the question was never put to him.
No BOLDED-details framing for the estimate email and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. The 'reply back to the email' line was offered as a booking channel, not as a detail check.
'Any other questions before I let you go?' never asked — on a shopping call, closing without that is leaving objections unsurfaced.
Business hours never given.
60 cents/lb baseline valuation never mentioned alongside No Worries, so the insurance explanation was only half complete.
No rapport or humor anywhere in the call — no name, no acknowledgment of moving stress, no lightness. The customer's 'Is there anything you're worried about?' moment never happened.
top_strength: Rance's technical estimating and objection handling were genuinely strong and are the reason this call scored where it did. He built the estimate transparently from a baseline and adjusted it with a real, teachable rule of thumb: 'Generally a two bedroom apartment move is gonna take two movers about three and a half to five and a half hours to complete however, in your case because we're going from the thirty second to the eighth floor. Those elevators do add quite a bit of time... it's about thirty minutes for every five floors is what we typically experience an elevator ads to the move.' When the customer pushed back that it was nearly double the time, Rance didn't retreat or hedge — he re-explained the mechanism (transport time, elevator capacity, reserved-elevator reality) and landed the same number. He also framed his own conservatism honestly rather than hiding it: 'I'm kind of, you know, being conservative with this estimate... I'd kind of rather, you know, give you good news at the end of the move then unexpected bad news.' That is exactly the estimate-accuracy posture the team is trying to build. His specialty-item probe was thorough and specific ('anything unusually, like, large bulky heavy, like a sleeper sofa. Like a large treadmill, an upright piano, gun safe?' then a second pass on fragile items that surfaced the marble coffee table and glass side table). And on the 30%-more-expensive objection he answered with substance instead of apology — all-in hourly, competitor hidden fees named one by one, twelve years of experience, '$2,000 damage coverage we provide on every move to repair, replace or reimburse for any kind of accidental damages,' and 'our movers are all well vetted, well trained, hourly employees. We don't use any daily contract Ted labors' — which landed well enough that the customer summarized the value prop back to him correctly and unprompted.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Rance won the argument and lost the call. He handled a 30% price objection well, the customer explicitly said 'I really wanted to do this with you guys,' and Rance let him hang up to go call competitors without ever attempting a booking or mentioning that it costs nothing to hold the date. The line he needed, the moment Juan said he'd call back later today, was: 'Juan, I completely get shopping it — that's smart. Here's the thing though: there's no deposit and no commitment to hold a date, so let me put that Sunday the 13th on the schedule right now at no charge. Finish your calls, and if someone beats us, just reply to the email and I'll release it — no hard feelings. That way if you do pick us, the date is still there instead of gone.' That single move converts a shopping call into a soft booking and costs Einstein nothing. Second priority: the Save Your Ass speech. Juan volunteered that he's moving a lot himself because the new place is close by — that is the single best opening for prep coaching on the board, and on an 8-9 hour elevator move at $210/hr every hour Juan removes is $210 back in his pocket, which is also the direct answer to 'you're 30% more expensive.' Rance should have said: 'Since you're already taking loads over yourself, let me make that count. Every carload you move — kids' stuff, closet items, loose things out of drawers, pictures off the walls, anything that fits in a car — comes straight off your bill at $210 an hour. Consolidate everything small into boxes stacked by the door before we get there, and honestly you could pull two or three hours off this estimate yourself. Does that make sense?' He also should have priced the option he recommended: he gave a total for the three-mover scenario but never for two movers, and left the customer audibly doing the math. Verify before the estimate email goes out: (1) The rate tier. Rance said 'it's Tuesday, 210 an hour,' but the call was Sunday 9/6 and the move on file is Sunday 9/13 — if Einstein's weekend tier differs, the whole quote including the $2,047 figure is wrong and the estimate email will lock in a bad number. (2) COI and dock/elevator reservations for both 215 Brazos and 101 Colorado. Juan raised the reserved elevator himself and got only 'Yup' — nobody confirmed who reserves it, for what window, or whether either building requires a certificate of insurance. On a 32nd-floor origin, a missing COI or an unreserved freight elevator is a failed move day, not a delay. (3) An 8-9 hour two-mover job is a long day with real fatigue and window risk; Rance correctly noted three movers lands 'about the same' price in 6-7 hours, and that should be the recommended configuration in EMMA, not the fallback. Finally, the basics cost him 15 points that require no skill at all: get and use the customer's name, return the 'how are you,' set the agenda with a 'sound good?', explain when the clock starts, and ask 'any other questions before I let you go?' Rance clearly knows the product cold — the gap here is entirely call structure and the ask, not knowledge.
phone_presence_notes: Knowledgeable, patient and confident under a direct price challenge — he explained rather than defended — but the warmth was thin: Juan's name is never used once, the customer's opening 'how are you?' goes unreturned, transitions are heavy on filler ('Okay. Okay. Okay.') and dead-air math ('Sorry, one moment. I'm doing some math here'), and there is no humor or rapport moment anywhere in the call.
